root_theorem.statement_nl: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \\geq 2$. For a sequence $s = (s_1,\\dots,s_{n-1})$ where each $s_i = \\pm 1$, let $f(s)$ be the number of permutations $(a_1,\\dots,a_n)$ of $\\{1,2,\\dots,n\\}$ such that $s_i(a_{i+1}-a_i) > 0$ for all $i$. For each $n$, determine the sequences $s$ for which $f(s)$ is maximal.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \\geq 2$. For a sequence $s = (s_1,\\dots,s_{n-1})$ where each $s_i = \\pm 1$, let $f(s)$ be the number of permutations $(a_1,\\dots,a_n)$ of $\\{1,2,\\dots,n\\}$ such that $s_i(a_{i+1}-a_i) > 0$ for all $i$. For each $n$, determine the sequences $s$ for which $f(s)$ is maximal.

selected_decomposition.strategy_summary: Use the standard recursion obtained by placing the largest entry n at a peak position of the sign pattern, compare every pattern to the alternating pattern through an induction on n, and isolate the only extremizers by analyzing when equality can occur in the inductive upper bound. The key quantitative input is a weighted independent-set inequality for the Euler up/down numbers.

steps.derives: Define A_n to be the common value of f(alt_plus(n)) and f(alt_minus(n)). By L3 this is well-defined, and by L4 the sequence A_n satisfies the alternating convolution recurrence A_n = sum_{k odd} binomial(n-1,k-1) A_{k-1}A_{n-k} = sum_{k even} binomial(n-1,k-1) A_{k-1}A_{n-k}.
steps.trivial_justification: This step packages the extremal benchmark and records the exact recurrence that will be used later.

steps.derives: For every m >= 1 and every sign sequence r of length m-1, one has f(r) <= A_m. In particular, for the fixed n in the theorem and every sign sequence s of length n-1, f(s) <= A_n.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply the universal upper-bound lemma L6 with m=n.

steps.derives: Both alternating sign sequences alt_plus(n) and alt_minus(n) attain the value A_n, since by definition A_n=f(alt_plus(n)) and by L3 also f(alt_minus(n))=A_n.
steps.trivial_justification: Direct substitution from the definition of A_n and the equality of the two alternating counts.

steps.derives: If a sign sequence s of length n-1 is maximal for f among all sign sequences, then f(s)=A_n and therefore s must be alternating, namely s=alt_plus(n) or s=alt_minus(n).
steps.trivial_justification: By A2, maximality implies f(s) cannot exceed A_n; by A3 the value A_n is attained, so a maximal sequence must satisfy f(s)=A_n. Then L7 forces s to be one of the two alternating sequences.

steps.derives: For every n >= 2, the sequences s for which f(s) is maximal are exactly the two alternating sign sequences: s_i=+1 for odd i and s_i=-1 for even i, or s_i=-1 for odd i and s_i=+1 for even i.
steps.trivial_justification: A3 shows both alternating sequences are maximal because they attain A_n, and A4 shows no other sequence can be maximal. This is exactly the root theorem statement.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: First isolate the benchmark value A_n coming from an alternating pattern and note that both alternating patterns have the same count. Next use induction on the size m to prove the universal upper bound f(r) <= A_m for every pattern r. For the inductive step, decompose f(r) by the position of the largest entry using L1; the admissible positions form an independent set by L2. Replace each smaller factor f(prefix) and f(suffix) by the corresponding alternating bounds A_{size} using the induction hypothesis, and then apply the weighted independent-set inequality L5 to conclude f(r) <= A_m. This proves that A_n is the maximum possible value. Finally, if equality f(s)=A_n holds, use L7 to deduce that every inequality in the induction must have been sharp, forcing the peak set at each stage to be a full parity class and recursively forcing s itself to alternate. Since the two alternating sequences do attain A_n, they are exactly the maximizers.

lemmas.statement_nl:
Let n >= 2 and let s=(s_1,...,s_{n-1}) be a sign sequence with each s_i in {+1,-1}. Define Peak(s) = { k in {1,...,n} : (k=1 or s_{k-1}=+1) and (k=n or s_k=-1) }. Then
f(s) = sum over k in Peak(s) of [binomial(n-1,k-1) * f((s_1,...,s_{k-2})) * f((s_{k+1},...,s_{n-1}))],
where an empty sign sequence contributes f(empty)=1. In words: if the largest value n is placed at position k, then k must lie in Peak(s), one chooses which k-1 values lie to the left of n, the left block realizes the prefix pattern (s_1,...,s_{k-2}), and the right block realizes the suffix pattern (s_{k+1},...,s_{n-1}).

domain_restrictions: n is an integer and n ≥ 2
s is a sequence of length n-1 with entries in {+1,-1}
Peak(s) is a subset of {1,...,n} defined by: k ∈ Peak(s) iff (k=1 or s_{k-1}=+1) and (k=n or s_k=-1)
Indices in prefix and suffix are empty when the start index exceeds the end index (convention: empty sequence allowed)
f is assumed defined for all sign sequences of lengths 0,1,...,n-1 (recursive use requires values for strictly shorter lengths)
Binomial coefficient C(n-1,k-1) is used only for integer parameters with 0 ≤ k-1 ≤ n-1
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim:
For every integer n ≥ 2 and every sign sequence s ∈ {+1,-1}^{n-1}, define Peak(s) := { k ∈ {1,...,n} : (k=1 or s_{k-1}=+1) and (k=n or s_k=-1) }. Assume f is defined on all sign sequences of lengths 0,...,n-1 with f(empty)=1. For each k ∈ Peak(s) define prefix_k := (s_1,...,s_{k-2}) with the convention that prefix_k is the empty sequence when k≤1, and define suffix_k := (s_{k+1},...,s_{n-1}) with the convention that suffix_k is empty when k≥n. Then
f(s) = Σ_{k ∈ Peak(s)} C(n-1,k-1) · f(prefix_k) · f(suffix_k),
where C(n-1,k-1) is the binomial coefficient (valid because 0 ≤ k-1 ≤ n-1). This equality recursively determines f(s) in terms of values of f on shorter sign sequences.
quantifier_order: For all integers n ≥ 2
For all sign sequences s ∈ {+1,-1}^{n-1}
Define Peak(s) ⊆ {1,...,n} by the given boolean condition on s
For each k ∈ Peak(s) (i.e. for each k ∈ {1,...,n} satisfying the Peak condition) the terms prefix_k and suffix_k are defined as above and contribute to the sum

lemmas.proof_nl:
Let A(s) be the set of all permutations a=(a_1,...,a_n) of {1,...,n} such that s_i(a_{i+1}-a_i)>0 for every i=1,...,n-1. Then f(s)=|A(s)|.

For each k in {1,...,n}, let A_k={a in A(s): a_k=n}. Since the largest value n occurs in exactly one position, the sets A_k are pairwise disjoint and their union is A(s). Hence f(s)=sum from k=1 to n of |A_k|.

If A_k is nonempty, choose a in A_k. If k>1, then a_k-a_{k-1}=n-a_{k-1}>0, so from the defining condition at i=k-1 we get s_{k-1}(n-a_{k-1})>0, which forces s_{k-1}=+1. If k<n, then a_{k+1}-a_k=a_{k+1}-n<0, so from the condition at i=k we get s_k(a_{k+1}-n)>0, which forces s_k=-1. Therefore A_k is empty unless (k=1 or s_{k-1}=+1) and (k=n or s_k=-1), i.e. unless k is in Peak(s). Thus f(s)=sum over k in Peak(s) of |A_k|.

Now fix k in Peak(s). For each subset L of {1,...,n-1} with |L|=k-1, let R be the complement of L in {1,...,n-1}, and let A_{k,L}={a in A_k : {a_1,...,a_{k-1}}=L}. Then A_k is the disjoint union of the sets A_{k,L} over all such L, so it suffices to compute |A_{k,L}|.

Write L={l_1<...<l_{k-1}} if k>1, and L=empty if k=1. Write R={r_1<...<r_{n-k}} if k<n, and R=empty if k=n. Let iota_L be the unique increasing bijection from {1,...,k-1} to L, and let iota_R be the unique increasing bijection from {1,...,n-k} to R; in the empty cases these are the unique empty maps.

Let P be the set counted by f((s_1,...,s_{k-2})): if k=1, P consists of the single empty sequence; if k>1, P consists of all permutations alpha=(alpha_1,...,alpha_{k-1}) of {1,...,k-1} such that s_i(alpha_{i+1}-alpha_i)>0 for i=1,...,k-2. Likewise, let Q be the set counted by f((s_{k+1},...,s_{n-1})): if k=n, Q consists of the single empty sequence; if k<n, Q consists of all permutations beta=(beta_1,...,beta_{n-k}) of {1,...,n-k} such that s_{k+t}(beta_{t+1}-beta_t)>0 for t=1,...,n-k-1. Therefore |P|=f((s_1,...,s_{k-2})) and |Q|=f((s_{k+1},...,s_{n-1})).

Define a map Phi_L from P x Q to A_{k,L} by setting a_i=iota_L(alpha_i) for 1<=i<=k-1, a_k=n, and a_{k+t}=iota_R(beta_t) for 1<=t<=n-k.

This map is well defined. Indeed, the entries on the left are exactly the elements of L, the entries on the right are exactly the elements of R, and a_k=n, so the resulting sequence is a permutation of {1,...,n}. Also, because iota_L and iota_R are increasing, they preserve the sign of each difference. Hence for 1<=i<=k-2, the sign of a_{i+1}-a_i is the same as the sign of alpha_{i+1}-alpha_i, so the left internal inequalities are exactly those encoded by (s_1,...,s_{k-2}). Similarly, for 1<=t<=n-k-1, the sign of a_{k+t+1}-a_{k+t} is the same as the sign of beta_{t+1}-beta_t, so the right internal inequalities are exactly those encoded by (s_{k+1},...,s_{n-1}). At the boundary, since k is in Peak(s), we have s_{k-1}=+1 when k>1 and s_k=-1 when k<n. Because every element of L and R is < n, we have a_{k-1}<n=a_k when k>1 and a_{k+1}<n=a_k when k<n, so the conditions at indices k-1 and k are automatically satisfied. Therefore Phi_L(P x Q) is contained in A_{k,L}.

Phi_L is bijective. Given a in A_{k,L}, define alpha_i=iota_L^{-1}(a_i) for i=1,...,k-1 and beta_t=iota_R^{-1}(a_{k+t}) for t=1,...,n-k. Since iota_L^{-1} and iota_R^{-1} are also increasing, the same sign-preservation argument shows that alpha lies in P and beta lies in Q. This construction is clearly inverse to Phi_L. So |A_{k,L}|=|P||Q|=f((s_1,...,s_{k-2})) f((s_{k+1},...,s_{n-1})).

There are exactly binomial(n-1,k-1) choices for L. Hence |A_k|=binomial(n-1,k-1) f((s_1,...,s_{k-2})) f((s_{k+1},...,s_{n-1})).

Summing over k in Peak(s), we obtain
f(s)=sum over k in Peak(s) of [binomial(n-1,k-1) * f((s_1,...,s_{k-2})) * f((s_{k+1},...,s_{n-1}))].

Finally, the prefix (s_1,...,s_{k-2}) has length max(k-2,0) and the suffix (s_{k+1},...,s_{n-1}) has length max(n-k-1,0), both strictly smaller than n-1, and the empty cases contribute f(empty)=1 by hypothesis. So the displayed identity indeed recursively determines f(s) from values of f on shorter sign sequences. This proves the lemma.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let n >= 2 and let s=(s_1,...,s_{n-1}) be a sign sequence with each s_i in {+1,-1}. Define Peak(s) = { k in {1,...,n} : (k=1 or s_{k-1}=+1) and (k=n or s_k=-1) }. Then Peak(s) contains no two consecutive integers. Equivalently, if k is in Peak(s), then k+1 is not in Peak(s).

domain_restrictions: n is an integer and n >= 2
s is a tuple (s_1,...,s_{n-1}) of length n-1 with each s_i ∈ {+1,-1}
Peak(s) ⊆ {1,...,n} by definition
When checking adjacency (k and k+1), restrict k to 1 ≤ k ≤ n-1 so that k+1 ∈ {2,...,n}
References to s_{k-1} occur only when k ≥ 2; references to s_k occur only when k ≤ n-1; these are guarded in the definition by the disjunctions (k=1 or ...) and (k=n or ...)
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all integers n >= 2 and for all sequences s ∈ {+1,-1}^{n-1}, there does not exist k ∈ {1,...,n-1} such that both k ∈ Peak(s) and k+1 ∈ Peak(s). Equivalently: for all n >= 2, for all s ∈ {+1,-1}^{n-1}, for all k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n-1, if ( (k=1 or s_{k-1}=+1) and (k=n or s_k=-1) ) then NOT( ( (k+1=1 or s_k=+1) and (k+1=n or s_{k+1}=-1) ) ).
quantifier_order: forall n ∈ Z, n >= 2
(equivalently) forall k ∈ {1,...,n-1} when asserting 'no two consecutive' property

lemmas.proof_nl:
We prove that no two consecutive integers can both lie in Peak(s).

By definition,
Peak(s) = { k in {1,...,n} : (k=1 or s_{k-1}=+1) and (k=n or s_k=-1) }.

Suppose for contradiction that there exists k with 1 <= k <= n-1 such that both k and k+1 belong to Peak(s).

Since k in Peak(s) and k <= n-1, the second condition in the definition of Peak(s) for the index k cannot be satisfied by k=n, so it must be satisfied by s_k=-1.

Since k+1 in Peak(s) and k+1 >= 2, the first condition in the definition of Peak(s) for the index k+1 cannot be satisfied by k+1=1, so it must be satisfied by s_k=+1.

Thus we obtain simultaneously s_k=-1 and s_k=+1, a contradiction.

Therefore there is no k in {1,...,n-1} such that both k and k+1 are in Peak(s). Hence Peak(s) contains no two consecutive integers.

This also yields the stated equivalent form: if k in Peak(s), then k+1 notin Peak(s). Indeed, if k=n then k+1=n+1 is not even an element of {1,...,n}, so certainly k+1 notin Peak(s); and if k<=n-1, the argument above shows k+1 cannot also lie in Peak(s).

So the lemma is proved.

lemmas.statement_nl: For m >= 1, let E_m = f(alt_plus(m)) and let F_m = f(alt_minus(m)), where alt_plus(m) is the alternating sign sequence (+1,-1,+1,-1,...) of length m-1 and alt_minus(m) is the alternating sign sequence (-1,+1,-1,+1,...) of length m-1. Then E_m = F_m for every m >= 1. In particular, both alternating sign sequences of a fixed length have the same number of realizing permutations.

domain_restrictions: m is an integer and m >= 1
alt_plus(m) and alt_minus(m) are defined as sequences of length m-1 (the case m=1 gives the empty sequence of length 0)
f must be defined on sign sequences of length m-1 for every m >= 1 (i.e. domain of f includes sequences of all lengths >= 0)

If f interprets 'realizing permutations', then f(s) refers to permutations of size |s|+1 that realize sign sequence s; in that interpretation, permutations considered are of size m when s has length m-1
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Given a fixed function f defined on sign sequences of all finite lengths, for every integer m >= 1 define alt_plus(m) = (+1,-1,+1,-1,...) of length m-1 and alt_minus(m) = (-1,+1,-1,+1,...) of length m-1, and let E_m := f(alt_plus(m)), F_m := f(alt_minus(m)). Then for all integers m >= 1 we have E_m = F_m. Equivalently, interpreting f(s) as the number of permutations of size |s|+1 that realize the sign sequence s, for every m >= 1 the number of permutations of [m] with up-down pattern alt_plus(m) equals the number with pattern alt_minus(m).
quantifier_order: f is fixed (implicit universal/background object; domain: sign sequences of all finite lengths)
for all integers m with m >= 1

If equality is interpreted as equality of sets, then the identity of elements would require a stronger claim (a structural bijection or equality of sets), and any witness (bijection or explicit identification) would again potentially depend on m.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Using the definition of f from the root theorem, for each m >= 1 and each sign sequence s of length m-1, f(s) is the number of permutations a = (a_1,...,a_m) of {1,...,m} such that s_i(a_{i+1} - a_i) > 0 for all i.

Fix m >= 1. Let s = alt_plus(m), and let t = alt_minus(m). By construction, t_i = -s_i for every i; equivalently, t = -s.

Let A_s be the set of permutations of {1,...,m} realizing s, and let A_t be the set of permutations of {1,...,m} realizing t. Then E_m = |A_s| and F_m = |A_t|.

Define a map T on permutations of {1,...,m} by
T(a_1,...,a_m) = (m+1-a_1, ..., m+1-a_m).
Because x -> m+1-x is a bijection of {1,...,m}, T indeed sends permutations of {1,...,m} to permutations of {1,...,m}.

Now take any a = (a_1,...,a_m) in A_s. For each i = 1,...,m-1,
T(a)_{i+1} - T(a)_i = (m+1-a_{i+1}) - (m+1-a_i) = -(a_{i+1} - a_i).
Therefore
 t_i (T(a)_{i+1} - T(a)_i)
= (-s_i)(-(a_{i+1} - a_i))
= s_i(a_{i+1} - a_i)
> 0.
So T(a) realizes t, i.e. T(a) is in A_t.

The same computation shows that if b is in A_t, then T(b) is in A_s. Also T(T(a)) = a for every permutation a, so T is its own inverse. Hence T is a bijection between A_s and A_t.

Consequently, |A_s| = |A_t|, that is,
E_m = f(alt_plus(m)) = f(alt_minus(m)) = F_m.

Thus for every m >= 1, the two alternating sign sequences of length m-1 have the same number of realizing permutations. (For m = 1 both sign sequences are empty, and the same argument still works.)
lemmas.role_in_parent: Lets us speak of a single alternating extremal value for size m.

lemmas.statement_nl:
Let n >= 2. Define A_n = f(alt_plus(n)), where alt_plus(n)=(+1,-1,+1,-1,...) has length n-1. Then
A_n = sum over odd k with 1 <= k <= n of [binomial(n-1,k-1) * A_{k-1} * A_{n-k}].
Also, using the other alternating pattern alt_minus(n), one has the equivalent recurrence
A_n = sum over even k with 1 <= k <= n of [binomial(n-1,k-1) * A_{k-1} * A_{n-k}].

domain_restrictions: n is an integer with n >= 2 (recurrence asserted for such n).
k is an integer with 1 <= k <= n; parity condition applied: 'odd k' or 'even k' as specified.
A_m must be defined for all indices m appearing in the recurrence, i.e. for all m in {0,1,...,n}; in particular A_0 must be defined.
f must be defined on alternating sign sequences of length L for all lengths L needed (here L = m-1 for m indices used to define A_m), in particular for lengths 0 up to n-1.
The codomain R of f must support addition and multiplication so the sum and product in the recurrence are meaningful (e.g. R a commutative ring or field).
Binomial(n-1,k-1) is used in the usual combinatorial sense and requires 0 <= k-1 <= n-1 (automatic from 1 <= k <= n).
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim:
For every integer n >= 2, assuming f is defined on alternating sign sequences of length n-1 and A_m are defined for 0 <= m <= n with values in a commutative ring R, define A_n := f(alt_plus(n)). Then
A_n = \sum_{k=1..n, k odd} \binom{n-1}{k-1} * A_{k-1} * A_{n-k}.
Similarly, if instead one defines A_n := f(alt_minus(n)) (same domain/codomain assumptions), then for every integer n >= 2
A_n = \sum_{k=1..n, k even} \binom{n-1}{k-1} * A_{k-1} * A_{n-k}.
(Here sums are over integers k in [1,n] meeting the parity constraint; all A_j appearing must be pre-defined.)
quantifier_order: For all integers n with n >= 2,

assume f is defined on sign-sequences of length n-1 and that A_m are defined for all m with 0 <= m <= n (values in R), with A_n := f(alt_plus(n)) in the first statement (or A_n := f(alt_minus(n)) in the second statement).

Then for that fixed n, for all integers k with 1 <= k <= n satisfying the stated parity constraint (odd for alt_plus-recurrence, even for alt_minus-recurrence), the term binomial(n-1,k-1) * A_{k-1} * A_{n-k} is formed and the sum over those k equals A_n.

The allowed index set for the sum (which k are included) depends on the parity requirement (odd or even) and on the fixed n.
Existence of A_0 (the witness for index 0) is required because k may be 1 in the sum, producing A_{k-1}=A_0.

lemmas.proof_nl:
For each m >= 1, let
U_m = f(alt_plus(m)) = number of permutations b_1,...,b_m of {1,...,m} satisfying b_1 < b_2 > b_3 < ...,
and let
D_m = f(alt_minus(m)) = number of permutations b_1,...,b_m of {1,...,m} satisfying b_1 > b_2 < b_3 > ... .
Also set U_0 = D_0 = 1, corresponding to the unique empty permutation; this is the A_0 appearing when one side of the distinguished entry is empty. In the first recurrence below, A_m means U_m; in the second, A_m means D_m.

First note that U_m = D_m for every m. Indeed, the map
(b_1,...,b_m) -> (m+1-b_1,...,m+1-b_m)
is a bijection from permutations with pattern < > < > ... to permutations with pattern > < > < ... , because x < y iff m+1-x > m+1-y. So the two alternating patterns give the same count for each size m.

Now fix n >= 2 and prove the first recurrence for U_n. Consider a permutation a = (a_1,...,a_n) counted by U_n, so
a_1 < a_2 > a_3 < a_4 > ... .
Let a_k = 1. Then k must be odd. If k is even and k < n, then since k is even the defining inequalities give a_k > a_{k+1}, impossible because a_k = 1 is the smallest entry. If k = n is even, then n-1 is odd and the defining inequalities give a_{n-1} < a_n = 1, again impossible.

Fix an odd k. We count the permutations counted by U_n with a_k = 1.
Choose the set L = {a_1,...,a_{k-1}} of entries to the left of 1. It may be any (k-1)-subset of {2,...,n}, so there are C(n-1,k-1) choices. Once L is chosen, the set on the right is forced: it is the complement of L in {2,...,n}.

For the left block (a_1,...,a_{k-1}), replace its smallest entry by 1, its next-smallest by 2, and so on. This standardization preserves all order comparisons, so the standardized left block is a permutation of {1,...,k-1} still satisfying
x_1 < x_2 > x_3 < ... ;
hence there are U_{k-1} possibilities for the left block.

For the right block (a_{k+1},...,a_n), standardization again preserves all order comparisons. Since k is odd, the comparisons among the right-block entries begin with
a_{k+1} > a_{k+2} < a_{k+3} > ... ,
so the standardized right block is counted by D_{n-k}. The inequalities adjacent to 1 are automatic: if k > 1 then a_{k-1} > 1, and if k < n then 1 < a_{k+1}, because every other entry lies in {2,...,n}.

Conversely, given:
1) a set L subseteq {2,...,n} with |L| = k-1,
2) an up-down permutation of {1,...,k-1}, and
3) a down-up permutation of {1,...,n-k},
there is a unique permutation of {1,...,n} with 1 in position k obtained by replacing ranks in the left block by the elements of L in increasing order and ranks in the right block by the remaining elements in increasing order. Because order-preserving relabeling preserves all inequalities, this reconstruction is valid and inverse to the previous decomposition.

Therefore, for each odd k, the number of permutations counted by U_n with a_k = 1 is exactly
C(n-1,k-1) U_{k-1} D_{n-k}.
Summing over all odd k gives
U_n = sum over odd k, 1 <= k <= n, of C(n-1,k-1) U_{k-1} D_{n-k}.
Using U_{n-k} = D_{n-k}, this becomes
U_n = sum over odd k, 1 <= k <= n, of C(n-1,k-1) U_{k-1} U_{n-k},
which is the first stated recurrence.

Now prove the second recurrence for D_n. Consider a permutation a = (a_1,...,a_n) counted by D_n, so
a_1 > a_2 < a_3 > a_4 < ... .
Let a_k = 1. Then k must be even. If k = 1, the inequality a_1 > a_2 is impossible. If k > 1 is odd, then k-1 is even, so the defining inequalities give a_{k-1} < a_k = 1, also impossible.

Fix an even k. Choose the set L = {a_1,...,a_{k-1}} on the left of 1; again there are C(n-1,k-1) choices. Standardizing the left block gives a permutation of {1,...,k-1} with pattern
x_1 > x_2 < x_3 > ... ,
so there are D_{k-1} possibilities. Since k is even, the comparisons among the right-block entries begin with
a_{k+1} > a_{k+2} < a_{k+3} > ... ,
so the standardized right block is also counted by D_{n-k}. The inequalities adjacent to 1 are automatic: if k > 1 then a_{k-1} > 1, and if k < n then 1 < a_{k+1}. The same reconstruction argument as above shows that, for each even k, the number of such permutations is exactly
C(n-1,k-1) D_{k-1} D_{n-k}.
Hence
D_n = sum over even k, 1 <= k <= n, of C(n-1,k-1) D_{k-1} D_{n-k},
which is the second stated recurrence.

Finally, since U_m = D_m for every m, the same numerical sequence may be denoted by A_m regardless of whether one starts from alt_plus or alt_minus. Thus, if A_n is defined via alt_plus, the odd-k convolution holds; if A_n is defined via alt_minus, the even-k convolution holds. This is exactly the lemma.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Provides the target extremal value and the exact convolution identity used in the induction.

lemmas.statement_nl:
For n >= 2, define weights w_n(k) = binomial(n-1,k-1) * A_{k-1} * A_{n-k} for 1 <= k <= n, where A_m = f(alt_plus(m)) for m >= 1. Let I be any subset of {1,...,n} containing no two consecutive integers. Then
sum over k in I of w_n(k) <= A_n.
Equivalently, among all independent subsets of the path graph on {1,...,n}, the total weight sum w_n(k) is maximized by one of the two parity classes, and that maximal value is exactly A_n.

domain_restrictions: n is integer with n >= 2
k is integer with 1 <= k <= n
A_m is explicitly defined only for m >= 1 in the text (A_m = f(alt_plus(m)) for m>=1); nonetheless w_n(k) uses A_{k-1} and A_{n-k} which can require A_0 when k=1 or k=n
binomial(n-1,k-1) uses standard combinatorial interpretation for integer arguments
I is any subset of {1,..,n} with no two consecutive integers (i.e. independent subset of the path graph on n vertices)
the statement implicitly treats A_m and w_n(k) as numeric (orderable) values so f ∘ alt_plus must take numeric values (real or at least nonnegative reals if sums are compared)
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integer n >= 2, suppose a sequence (A_m)_{m>=1} is given with A_m = f(alt_plus(m)). Define weights for k ∈ {1,..,n} by w_n(k) = C(n-1,k-1) * A_{k-1} * A_{n-k}, where C denotes the standard binomial coefficient. (Note: this formula references A_0 when k=1 or k=n; the statement below requires A_0 to be specified or interpreted.) Then for every subset I ⊆ {1,..,n} that contains no two consecutive integers, sum_{k∈I} w_n(k) ≤ A_n. Equivalently, the maximum of S(I) := sum_{k∈I} w_n(k) over all independent I ⊆ {1,..,n} equals max( sum_{k odd ≤ n} w_n(k), sum_{k even ≤ n} w_n(k) ), and this maximal value equals A_n. In particular, one of the two parity classes (odd indices or even indices) is a maximizer and attains the value A_n. (The choice of parity class may depend on n and on the sequence A_m.)
quantifier_order: For all integers n >= 2,
define A_m for m >= 1 by A_m = f(alt_plus(m)) (as given),
for all integers k with 1 <= k <= n define w_n(k) := binomial(n-1,k-1) * A_{k-1} * A_{n-k},
for all subsets I ⊆ {1,..,n} satisfying 'no two consecutive integers' (i.e. independent sets), the inequality sum_{k in I} w_n(k) <= A_n holds.

The equivalence/additional claim asserts existence: there exists an independent subset achieving equality; specifically one of the two parity classes (odd-indexed vertices or even-indexed vertices) attains the maximum. The choice of which parity class attains A_n may depend on n and on the whole sequence (A_m) (i.e. on the values of f(alt_plus(m))).
Each weight w_n(k) depends explicitly on A_{k-1} and A_{n-k}; thus any dependence of maxima on the sequence A_m is mediated through these factors.
A_n on the right-hand side depends on f(alt_plus(n)) (since n >= 2 so A_n is in the provided domain)

lemmas.proof_nl:
Let Alt_+(m) be the set of permutations x=(x_1,...,x_m) of {1,...,m} with x_1 < x_2 > x_3 < ... , and Alt_-(m) the set with x_1 > x_2 < x_3 > ... . For m >= 1, A_m = |Alt_+(m)|. Also put B_m = |Alt_-(m)|.

Extend both definitions by Alt_+(0)=Alt_-(0)={empty permutation}; hence A_0=B_0=1. This is the correct empty-permutation convention, because when 1 sits at the first or last position in an alternating permutation, one side of the decomposition is empty and should contribute exactly one possibility. The complement map x_i -> m+1-x_i is a bijection Alt_+(m) <-> Alt_-(m), so B_m=A_m for all m >= 0.

For odd k, let U_k = {pi in Alt_+(n) : pi_k = 1}. To build such a pi, choose the k-1 entries left of 1; there are C(n-1,k-1) choices. After standardizing, the left block is an element of Alt_+(k-1), and the right block is an element of Alt_-(n-k). Conversely, these data determine pi uniquely. Therefore |U_k| = C(n-1,k-1) A_{k-1} B_{n-k} = C(n-1,k-1) A_{k-1} A_{n-k} = w_n(k).

Similarly, for even k, if V_k = {pi in Alt_-(n) : pi_k = 1}, then by the same argument |V_k| = C(n-1,k-1) B_{k-1} A_{n-k} = C(n-1,k-1) A_{k-1} A_{n-k} = w_n(k).

Hence
sum over odd k of w_n(k) = |Alt_+(n)| = A_n,
and
sum over even k of w_n(k) = |Alt_-(n)| = B_n = A_n.
So each parity class is an independent set of total weight A_n.

Now define, for 1 <= i <= n-1, a set C_i of permutations b=(b_1,...,b_{n-1}) of {1,...,n-1} by the rule:
for 1 <= j <= n-2,
b_j < b_{j+1} iff j is odd when j < i, and iff j is even when j >= i.
Thus the comparison signs alternate, except that the phase changes at i. In particular C_1 = Alt_-(n-1) and C_{n-1} = Alt_+(n-1). Let c_i = |C_i|, and set c_0=c_n=0.

Also let D_i be the complement image of C_i; equivalently, d=(d_1,...,d_{n-1}) lies in D_i iff d_j < d_{j+1} iff j is even when j < i, and iff j is odd when j >= i. Since complement reverses every comparison, |D_i|=|C_i|=c_i.

Claim: w_n(k)=c_{k-1}+c_k for every k.

First let k be odd. Delete the entry 1 from a permutation pi in U_k and subtract 1 from all remaining entries. For j < k-1 the comparison signs are unchanged, so they are the usual up-down signs. For j >= k the signs are shifted by one place, so they are rise exactly when j is even. At the middle place j=k-1 the comparison can be either rise or fall. Therefore the resulting permutation lies in C_{k-1} if b_{k-1} < b_k, and in C_k if b_{k-1} > b_k. (For k=1 or k=n, only C_1 or C_{n-1} occurs; this is exactly the boundary convention c_0=c_n=0.) Conversely, if b lies in C_{k-1} or C_k, then after adding 1 to every entry and inserting 1 at position k, the inserted 1 creates the required valley and repairs the phase change, so the result is an element of U_k. Hence |U_k| = c_{k-1}+c_k, and therefore w_n(k)=c_{k-1}+c_k for odd k.

Now let k be even. The same deletion/insertion argument, applied to V_k and to the sets D_{k-1}, D_k, shows that |V_k| = |D_{k-1}| + |D_k| = c_{k-1}+c_k. Since |V_k|=w_n(k), we again get w_n(k)=c_{k-1}+c_k.

So for every k with 1 <= k <= n,
w_n(k)=c_{k-1}+c_k.

Now sum this identity over odd k. Each c_i with 1 <= i <= n-1 appears exactly once in the sum of c_{k-1}+c_k over odd k, so
sum from i=1 to n-1 of c_i = sum over odd k of w_n(k) = A_n.
Because c_0=c_n=0, this is the same as
sum from i=0 to n of c_i = A_n.

Finally, let I be any subset of {1,...,n} with no two consecutive integers. Then
sum over k in I of w_n(k) = sum over k in I of (c_{k-1}+c_k).
Since I is independent, the sets {k-1,k} for k in I are pairwise disjoint subsets of {0,...,n}. Therefore
sum over k in I of (c_{k-1}+c_k) <= sum from i=0 to n of c_i = A_n.
Thus
sum over k in I of w_n(k) <= A_n.

This proves the required inequality. Since the odd-index set and the even-index set are both independent and each has total weight A_n, the maximum independent-set weight is exactly A_n. In fact both parity classes attain it; in particular one of them is a maximizer.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Key comparison inequality that turns the general recursion into the extremal bound f(s) <= A_n.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let n >= 1 and let A_n = f(alt_plus(n)). For every integer m with 1 <= m <= n and every sign sequence r of length m-1 with entries in {+1,-1}, one has f(r) <= A_m. In other words, for each size m up to n, the alternating pattern count A_m is an upper bound for all sign patterns of length m-1.

A_k is defined by A_k = f(alt_plus(k)) for each k in {1,...,n}
The codomain of f is equipped with a total order so that ≤ is meaningful (implicitly: real numbers or ordered set)

lemmas.proof_nl: Fix m >= 1. It is enough to prove the stronger statement that for every sign sequence r of length m-1, one has f(r) <= A_m; then the lemma for all m <= n follows immediately. For a sign sequence s of length m-1, define E_s = { (x_1,...,x_m) in [0,1]^m : s_i (x_{i+1} - x_i) > 0 for every 1 <= i <= m-1 }. The regions x_{pi(1)} < x_{pi(2)} < ... < x_{pi(m)} (pi a permutation of {1,...,m}) partition [0,1]^m up to the measure-zero set where two coordinates are equal, and each such region has volume 1/m!. Exactly f(s) of these regions lie inside E_s, so vol(E_s) = f(s)/m!. For x in [0,1], let g_s(x) be the (m-1)-dimensional volume of the section { (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) : (x_1,...,x_{m-1},x) belongs to E_s }. Then f(s) = m! * integral from 0 to 1 of g_s(x) dx. Also, by Fubini, these section functions satisfy the recursion g_empty(x) = 1, g_{t,+}(x) = integral from 0 to x of g_t(y) dy, and g_{t,-}(x) = integral from x to 1 of g_t(y) dy. Now let u_m be the unique alternating sign sequence of length m-1 whose last sign is +, and let v_m be the unique alternating sign sequence of length m-1 whose last sign is -. Set U_m = g_{u_m} and V_m = g_{v_m}; for m=1 both sequences are empty, so U_1 = V_1 = 1. From the recursion just written, U_{m+1}(x) = integral from 0 to x of V_m(y) dy and V_{m+1}(x) = integral from x to 1 of U_m(y) dy. Hence U_m is increasing and V_m is decreasing. Moreover V_m(x) = U_m(1-x) for all m: this is true for m=1, and if it holds for m then V_{m+1}(x) = integral from x to 1 of U_m(y) dy = integral from 0 to 1-x of U_m(1-z) dz = integral from 0 to 1-x of V_m(z) dz = U_{m+1}(1-x). We now prove by induction on m >= 2 the following pointwise envelope statement: every sign sequence s of length m-1 ending with + satisfies g_s(x) <= U_m(x) for all x, and every sign sequence s of length m-1 ending with - satisfies g_s(x) <= V_m(x) for all x. For m=2 this is equality: g_(+)(x)=x=U_2(x) and g_(-)(x)=1-x=V_2(x). Assume the statement true for size m, and let s have length m and end with +. Write s = t,+, where t has length m-1. If t ends with -, then by induction g_t <= V_m, so g_s(x) = integral from 0 to x of g_t(y) dy <= integral from 0 to x of V_m(y) dy = U_{m+1}(x). If t ends with +, then g_t <= U_m, hence g_s(x) <= integral from 0 to x of U_m(y) dy. Since U_m is increasing, integral from 0 to x of U_m(y) dy <= integral from 0 to x of U_m(y+1-x) dy = integral from 1-x to 1 of U_m(y) dy = integral from 0 to x of V_m(y) dy = U_{m+1}(x). Thus every sequence ending with + is bounded by U_{m+1}. The proof for sequences ending with - is analogous. If s = t,- and t ends with +, then g_s(x) <= integral from x to 1 of U_m(y) dy = V_{m+1}(x). If t ends with -, then g_s(x) <= integral from x to 1 of V_m(y) dy = integral from 0 to 1-x of V_m(y+x) dy <= integral from 0 to 1-x of V_m(y) dy = integral from x to 1 of U_m(y) dy = V_{m+1}(x), because V_m is decreasing. This completes the induction. Finally, alt_plus(m) is the alternating sequence starting with +. If m is even, it ends with +, so alt_plus(m) = u_m; if m is odd, it ends with -, so alt_plus(m) = v_m. Since V_m(x) = U_m(1-x), the integrals of U_m and V_m over [0,1] are equal. Therefore both numbers m! * integral U_m and m! * integral V_m are equal to A_m = f(alt_plus(m)). Now take any sign sequence r of length m-1. If m=1, then r is empty and f(r)=A_1=1. If r ends with +, then g_r <= U_m, hence f(r) = m! * integral g_r <= m! * integral U_m = A_m. If r ends with -, the same argument with V_m gives f(r) <= A_m. Thus for every m >= 1 and every sign sequence r of length m-1, one has f(r) <= A_m. This is exactly the desired bound.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Inductive global bound obtained from L1, L2, L4, and L5.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let n >= 2 and let s=(s_1,...,s_{n-1}) be a sign sequence with each s_i in {+1,-1}. Assume f(s)=A_n, where A_n=f(alt_plus(n)). Then s is alternating: either s_i=+1 for odd i and s_i=-1 for even i for all i, or s_i=-1 for odd i and s_i=+1 for even i for all i. Equivalently, the only sign sequences attaining the upper bound A_n are alt_plus(n) and alt_minus(n).

lemmas.proof_nl:
For each m >= 1 and each sign sequence sigma = (sigma_1,...,sigma_{m-1}) of length m-1, define a count vector C_sigma = (c_sigma(1),...,c_sigma(m)) by
c_sigma(j) = the number of permutations a = (a_1,...,a_m) of {1,...,m} such that sigma_i(a_{i+1}-a_i) > 0 for all i = 1,...,m-1 and a_m = j.
Then f(sigma) = sum_{j=1}^m c_sigma(j).

For a nonnegative vector x = (x_1,...,x_r), define two vectors of length r+1 by
P(x)_j = sum_{i=1}^{j-1} x_i,
and
S(x)_j = sum_{i=j}^r x_i.
These are the prefix-sum and suffix-sum operators.

If sigma = tau followed by +, then C_sigma = P(C_tau). If sigma = tau followed by -, then C_sigma = S(C_tau). Here is the proof of the first identity; the second is analogous. Fix j. Take a permutation of {1,...,m} realizing sigma and ending in j. Delete its last entry j, and subtract 1 from every remaining entry that is > j. This produces a permutation of {1,...,m-1}; all inequalities among the first m-1 positions are preserved, so the new permutation realizes tau. Moreover, because the last comparison was upward, the old penultimate entry was < j, hence after the relabeling the new last entry has some value i < j. Conversely, from any permutation of {1,...,m-1} realizing tau and ending with i < j, add 1 to every entry >= j and append j; then the last comparison is upward, so we recover a unique permutation realizing sigma and ending in j. Therefore c_sigma(j) = sum_{i<j} c_tau(i), i.e. C_sigma = P(C_tau). The minus case gives c_sigma(j) = sum_{i>=j} c_tau(i), i.e. C_sigma = S(C_tau).

Because P and S are given by sums with nonnegative coefficients, they preserve coordinatewise inequality on count vectors. They are also injective: if y = P(x), then x_k = y_{k+1} - y_k; if y = S(x), then x_k = y_k - y_{k+1}.

Now let alpha_m^+ and alpha_m^- be the two alternating sign sequences of length m-1, chosen so that alpha_m^+ ends with + and alpha_m^- ends with -. For the recursion we also set alpha_1^+ = alpha_1^- = the empty sequence. Then for m >= 2,
alpha_m^+ = alpha_{m-1}^- followed by +,
and
alpha_m^- = alpha_{m-1}^+ followed by -.
Define
U_m := C_{alpha_m^+},
D_m := C_{alpha_m^-}.
Then U_m = P(D_{m-1}) and D_m = S(U_{m-1}). In particular U_m is nondecreasing and D_m is nonincreasing, since they are obtained from count vectors by P and S.

Next, complement gives a symmetry. For a permutation a = (a_1,...,a_m), define a^c by a_i^c = m+1-a_i. If a realizes a sign pattern rho, then a^c realizes the negated pattern -rho, because every difference changes sign. Since alpha_m^- = - alpha_m^+, complement gives a bijection between realizers of alpha_m^+ ending in j and realizers of alpha_m^- ending in m+1-j. Hence
D_m(j) = U_m(m+1-j)
for every j, so D_m is exactly the reverse of U_m.

Also, complement swaps alt_plus(m) and alt_minus(m). Therefore those two alternating patterns have the same total count. Since A_m is defined as f(alt_plus(m)), both alternating patterns have total count A_m. Because {alpha_m^+, alpha_m^-} = {alt_plus(m), alt_minus(m)}, we get
sum_j U_m(j) = sum_j D_m(j) = A_m.
This is the only place where the definition of A_m is used.

We also need a positivity fact. Each alternating pattern has at least one realizing permutation: 1,m,2,m-1,3,... realizes alt_plus(m), and m,1,m-1,2,m-2,3,... realizes alt_minus(m). Hence f(alpha_r^+) > 0 and f(alpha_r^-) > 0 for every r >= 1. In particular, for m >= 3,
U_{m-1}(m-1) = sum_i D_{m-2}(i) = f(alpha_{m-2}^-) > 0.
By reversal, D_{m-1}(1) = U_{m-1}(m-1) > 0. Also U_{m-1}(1)=0 because U_{m-1}=P(D_{m-2}), and D_{m-1}(m-1)=0 because D_{m-1}=S(U_{m-2}).

We now prove by induction on m >= 2 the following stronger statement.

(+) For every sign sequence sigma of length m-1 ending with +, we have C_sigma <= U_m coordinatewise; moreover C_sigma = U_m iff sigma = alpha_m^+.

(-) For every sign sequence sigma of length m-1 ending with -, we have C_sigma <= D_m coordinatewise; moreover C_sigma = D_m iff sigma = alpha_m^-.

Base case m = 2. The only sign sequence ending with + is +, realized only by (1,2), so C_+ = (0,1) = U_2. The only sign sequence ending with - is -, realized only by (2,1), so C_- = (1,0) = D_2. Thus both statements hold.

Inductive step. Assume the claims for m-1, where m >= 3.

Proof of (+). Let sigma = tau followed by +.

Case 1: tau ends with -. By the inductive hypothesis, C_tau <= D_{m-1}. Applying P gives
C_sigma = P(C_tau) <= P(D_{m-1}) = U_m.
If equality holds, then by injectivity of P we get C_tau = D_{m-1}; the inductive hypothesis then yields tau = alpha_{m-1}^-, so sigma = alpha_m^+.

Case 2: tau ends with +. By induction, C_tau <= U_{m-1}. Hence
C_sigma = P(C_tau) <= P(U_{m-1}).
Now U_{m-1} is nondecreasing, and D_{m-1} is its reverse. Therefore, for each j,
P(U_{m-1})_j = sum_{i=1}^{j-1} U_{m-1}(i) <= sum_{i=m-j+1}^{m-1} U_{m-1}(i) = P(D_{m-1})_j = U_m(j),
because in a nondecreasing vector a prefix sum is at most the suffix sum of the same length. So C_sigma <= U_m.
Moreover this inequality is strict when j = m-1: if T = sum_{i=1}^{m-1} U_{m-1}(i), then
P(U_{m-1})_{m-1} = T - U_{m-1}(m-1) < T - U_{m-1}(1) = P(D_{m-1})_{m-1} = U_m(m-1),
since U_{m-1}(1)=0 and U_{m-1}(m-1)=f(alpha_{m-2}^-) > 0. Therefore C_sigma cannot equal U_m in this case. This proves (+).

Proof of (-). Let sigma = tau followed by -.

Case 1: tau ends with +. By induction, C_tau <= U_{m-1}. Applying S gives
C_sigma = S(C_tau) <= S(U_{m-1}) = D_m.
If equality holds, injectivity of S gives C_tau = U_{m-1}; hence tau = alpha_{m-1}^+ and sigma = alpha_m^-.

Case 2: tau ends with -. By induction, C_tau <= D_{m-1}. Hence
C_sigma = S(C_tau) <= S(D_{m-1}).
Now D_{m-1} is nonincreasing, and U_{m-1} is its reverse. Therefore, for each j,
S(D_{m-1})_j = sum_{i=j}^{m-1} D_{m-1}(i) <= sum_{i=1}^{m-j} D_{m-1}(i) = S(U_{m-1})_j = D_m(j),
because in a nonincreasing vector a suffix sum is at most the prefix sum of the same length. So C_sigma <= D_m.
Again the inequality is strict: if T = sum_{i=1}^{m-1} D_{m-1}(i), then at j = 2 we have
S(D_{m-1})_2 = T - D_{m-1}(1) < T - D_{m-1}(m-1) = S(U_{m-1})_2 = D_m(2),
since D_{m-1}(m-1)=0 and D_{m-1}(1)=U_{m-1}(m-1)=f(alpha_{m-2}^-) > 0. Hence equality cannot occur in this case. This proves (-).

The induction is complete.

Now let s be any sign sequence of length n-1 and assume f(s) = A_n. If s ends with +, the proved (+) statement gives C_s <= U_n. Summing coordinates,
A_n = f(s) = sum_j C_s(j) <= sum_j U_n(j) = A_n.
Hence all coordinatewise inequalities must actually be equalities, so C_s = U_n; by the equality part of (+), s = alpha_n^+.
If s ends with -, the same argument with (-) gives s = alpha_n^-.

Finally {alpha_n^+, alpha_n^-} = {alt_plus(n), alt_minus(n)}. Therefore s is alternating, namely s = alt_plus(n) or s = alt_minus(n). This is exactly the lemma.
